item.title: Hungary begins hunt for corrupt regime's billions
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.11
Asset recovery — it sounds bureaucratic but behind this phrase is one of the most important campaign promises made by Hungary's new government. Hungary's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, and his Tisza party want to retrieve funds and assets that went — in some dubious ways — to the family of ousted Hungarian leader Viktor Orban or his allies, various oligarchs, or frontmen. The new government wants those funds back for state use, and it also plans to hold the beneficiaries accountable under law. Billions of euros were stolen or diverted and, if social media is to be believed, many Hungarians want to see the individuals responsible behind bars. Magyar has talked of a sum of around €60 billion ($70 billion), though other estimates suggest the real amount could be three times that much. Orban, allies lived lives of luxury Observers say the success or failure of the asset recovery will almost certainly influence the future of Magyar and the Tisza party. The huge sums of money are linked to images of decadent luxury under Orban. The former Hungarian prime minister's family, party members, and friendly oligarchs lived on luxury estates, flew in luxury jets, vacationed on luxury yachts, and repeatedly won billions worth of public contracts. Orban-affiliated entrepreneurs, artists, academics, and journalists were also generously supported with public funds for years. Often their main qualification was loyalty to the former prime minister. Those lifestyles contrasted with the lives led by Hungarians in poverty, the image of neglected public infrastructure, poor conditions in schools and hospitals, and the exodus of many young Hungarians from the country, as well as a huge deficit in the state budget, some 7.5% of Hungary's national income. These contrasts explain why there is such a popular desire for justice. It's been almost four months since the new Magyar government took office and anti-corruption actions have officially started. At the end of July, the new government established the National Asset Recovery Authority, or NVVH — a sort of "super institution" with very broad powers and independence. Hungary hasn't had an authority like this in its modern history. The way state assets were privatized in the 1990s after communist rule was problematic, as it often was elsewhere in the former Soviet bloc. When Orban first came to power in 2010, there was a half-hearted attempt to address the corruption of the previous government under Ferenc Gyurcsany, but it came to nothing. This time, things are meant to be different. The NVVH will investigate where public funds flowed and how assets like real estate were used. Although no specific date has been set, the investigations will primarily focus on the Orban government's time in power, so dating back to 2010. The authority is also meant to make sure this cannot happen again, and will look into how public funds and assets are to be used in future. The NVVH has both policing and prosecutorial powers, so it can investigate cases and bring charges. The authority is accountable to Hungary's parliament. Controversy around new anti-corruption body But the creation of the NVVH has not been without controversy. Late last week, parliament appointed Anna Unger, 46, a political scientist at Eotvos Lorand University in Budapest, to head the new anti-corruption and asset recovery body. Unger is an expert on political systems, democratic institutions, and party financing and was chosen out of almost 100 other applicants in a process with several stages. Some were surprised at Unger's appointment, as she wasn't really a public figure. Her research has included political corruption but she's not a recognized expert on the topic, nor is she a lawyer. Observers had expected a lawyer or an anti-corruption expert to get the job, somebody like Miklos Ligeti, head of legal affairs at Transparency International Hungary since 2012. Ligeti also applied for the job but is reportedly being considered for a position as a deputy director. Unger will have four deputies with different duties and responsibilities. Katalin Tasnady, a well-known prosecutor with around two decades of criminal law experience, was made the NVVH's deputy chief of investigations. Government representatives said Unger had presented a comprehensive political vision for the agency's work. During her parliamentary hearing, she said that under Orban, Hungary saw more than just what one might call classic corruption. An almost feudal system had prevailed, she argued. That was why in addition to restitution and asset recovery, the system had to be thoroughly investigated and exposed so that it would never happen again, Unger said. No justice in next 6 years? Unger caused the biggest upset when she said it would be folly to expect legally binding verdicts in any major corruption cases during the NVVH's first six-year term. Robert Puzser, a popular commentator and personality on social media, called Unger's statement "devastating." Voters had given Magyar "unprecedented power to hold the country's plunderers to account," he said on Facebook, and if Hungarians had to wait more than six years, it could cause the collapse of this new government. The new prime minister himself reacted angrily to critics who said the NVVH should have had a lawyer at its head. "Nobody promised people they could vote for the leader of the NVVH as if it was a [reality TV] casting show," he wrote on Facebook. Plenty of experts thought Unger was absolutely suitable for the job. In a podcast on the 24.hu media outlet, political science Gabor Torok surmised that the way that the NVVH had been established indicated that it would be a "strong political institution" that aimed to come to terms with the recent past. Torok said the public expects the Tisza party to thoroughly reckon with the old system, and the new government will only be able to maintain the public's trust if it doesn't look like the "culprits of the previous order" are getting away with their past crimes, he said. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Ebola: Why children are last to be treated in medical crises
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.95
The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been devastating. Since the outbreak began in mid-May, more than 3,000 people have died. Almost half of people infected with Ebola are expected to die, and the mortality rate is particularly high for young children. According to a commentary by Doctors Without Borders recently published in medical journal The Lancet, the mortality rate for children under the age of 5 is over 60%. But often, it's because of a lack of medication and information on how to use it with young patients, rather than then disease itself. "Children must be centered in Ebola treatment and prevention research," the aid organization wrote in early September. At the heart of the debate is the EBO-PEP study, which began mid-July. The study looks at an experimental antiviral drug called obeldesivir, which is being studied for its ability to protect people exposed to the Bundibugyo Ebola virus, the strain responsible for the current deadly outbreak. But children weighing less than 30 kilograms (about 66 pounds) and around 12 years old or younger, were not included in the original study. But that could change soon with protocols to include children weighing over 20 kilograms. Children weighing less than 20 kilograms — that is, roughly 6 years old or younger — won't be included in the treatment. There is an alternative treatment for them: Another antiviral drug, remdesivir, given intravenously. But as Doctors Without Borders argued, a 10-day course of infusions is difficult to administer during an outbreak, especially for young children. According to Neal Russell, a pediatric doctor based in London who consults for Doctors Without Borders and who was also the lead author of the Lancet commentary, young children are at particularly high risk from Ebola. This could be due to their weakened immune systems, underlying health conditions, or the fact that treating them for Ebola is especially challenging in an outbreak. For example, children are often harder to diagnose than adults because early symptoms resemble other illnesses, and young children often find it difficult to describe their symptoms accurately. Other issues include the fact that children cannot always be accompanied into an Ebola treatment center by their parents or caregivers, something that is especially important in their recovery. Younger Ebola patients also require closer monitoring and specially trained staff. Ebola in Berlin In May, an American doctor was treated at Berlin's Charite hospital after contracting the Bundibugyo Ebola virus while caring for patients. His wife and their four children were also considered at high risk. The medical team in Germany decided to treat the family prophylactically with an experimental antibody drug called MBP134. "Of course, a careful risk benefit assessment had to be carried out," said Han Ngoc Le, a doctor at the hospital who was involved in the treatments. The available data about the drug's impact on children was very limited. But at the same time, the children were at high risk of catching Ebola after close contact with their sick father. In the end, all the family remained healthy and no apparent side effects were seen. It's unclear whether the experimental treatment prevented infection in the children. Such a small sample can't be mapped onto the larger population either. But the test was valuable nonetheless. "The mere fact that the antibody was so well tolerated even in 1-year-olds and children under 12 is a valuable finding upon which future studies can build," Le said. Why do such gaps in knowledge exist? Le explained that, from a medical perspective, children cannot simply be thought of as "small adults." Their metabolisms function differently, they react differently to medications, their pharmacokinetics — what a body does with a drug — are simply different. The same sort of cautions also apply to pregnant women. That's why dosages of medication can't simply be transferred from adults to children. It's also why any new medications require separate studies so that specific dosages can be determined and potentially special formulations can be developed. Children might require kid-friendly syrups instead of adult-size tablets, for example. "All of this creates extra costs," said Marc Biot, access coordinator for Europe at Doctors Without Borders, who works to ensure people in need can get affordable, good-quality medical products. He said research institutions and pharmaceutical companies often see investing extra in pediatric studies as a lower priority. "It is faster and it can be cheaper if you only focus on adults," said Biot — which is why treating children and pregnant women usually only becomes part of the research at a later stage of drug development. "That is our plea — a plea not only to the scientists, to the pharmaceutical companies, but also to those who fund and allow trials to happen — to allow that to happen on the same speed for adults as for children and pregnant women." Biot said it's sad to see that pressure is needed to make it happen. "Whenever you start a clinical trial, you also should include pregnant woman or children," he argued. A difficult balance None of this is new. In 2020, the Global Accelerator for Pediatric Formulations network was founded — supported by the World Health Organization(WHO) — to accelerate the development and availability of child-friendly medicine worldwide. This isn't an issue limited to Ebola. Russell pointed to the 2024 mpox epidemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where children made up a large proportion of those infected or killed. Although a vaccine existed for mpox, it wasn't made for children. The WHO advised it be used "off label" for minors, but they tended to get it a lot later than adults anyway. Experts say they've observed similar patterns with other diseases including HIV, tuberculosis, and during the COVID-19 pandemic. "When you're doing a research study, which is not in an emergency, [it makes sense] to protect children and pregnant women from any potential harm of an investigational product," said Russell. "But when you're in an emergency, the balance between protecting those people from any potential harm from research, and protecting them from the very fatal disease, changes." Berlin-based doctor Le believes children and pregnant women should be considered right from the beginning of any new clinical trials. "They shouldn't be excluded from participation just like that," she said. "Instead, sub-studies or parallel studies should be set up from the outset." Russell calls for a similar approach. He wants to see all people benefit equally from scientific progress during a health crisis — especially in a health emergency, when the most vulnerable should not be the last to benefit from that progress. "No matter who you are, you should have the same opportunity to have access to these medical products," he said. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: The Future of Ukraine’s Drone Democracy
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.54
On August 19, the Ukrainian parliament voted overwhelmingly to confirm Ukraine’s new defense minister, ending weeks of uncertainty at a crucial phase of the war. For more than a month, Ukrainians had taken to the streets of Kyiv and other cities to protest President Volodymyr Zelensky’s firing of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov. His successor, Yevhenii Khmara, is a special operations officer, best known for leading Operation Spider’s Web, the successful attack on Russian strategic bombers deep inside Russia. But the political fallout from this summer’s upheaval is not over. The removal of Fedorov, whom many Ukrainians considered highly effective, set off a series of decisions by Zelensky to reshuffle the cabinet, and more consequentially, the heads of military and law enforcement agencies. Shortly after dismissing his defense minister, Zelensky sought to quell the public backlash by also firing Oleksandr Syrsky, the unpopular commander of the armed forces. As a result, the president was simultaneously replacing the two figures—the defense minister and the head of the military—officially responsible for Ukraine’s defense against Russia. That this was happening at the very moment Ukraine was gaining the advantage on the battlefield has made the changes all the more fraught. For one thing, the large-scale protests themselves mark a new stage in Zelensky’s relationship to the electorate. Unlike any previous protests since the full-scale invasion, Ukrainians directly challenged the president’s handling of the war, introducing a dynamic that is unlikely to go away. Perhaps even more consequential, on the eve of the parliament’s vote on Fedorov’s successor, Fedorov released a controversial video address in which he declared that Ukraine needed a “system reboot” and called for wartime elections—the first time that not merely a prominent Ukrainian figure but a member of Zelensky’s inner circle and one of his former closest allies had done so. Until now, most Ukrainians have dismissed the prospect, since elections cannot be held while the country is under martial law. Amid these developments, something else has become increasingly clear: one of the unforeseen consequences of Ukraine’s transition to drone-centered warfare has been the expansion of civil society in new ways. The embrace of a decentralized, technology-driven defense strategy has required new forms of cooperation between military and civilians, giving far more people a stake in matters of national security and military strategy. And that has created a new reality for the country’s leadership. A DIFFERENT WAR A crucial factor driving the events of this summer is the evolution of the military confrontation with Russia into a drone war. This reality, which began to take hold in 2024, has accelerated Ukraine’s transition from foreign-supplied to domestically produced weapons: some 95 percent of drones are now assembled inside the country. Moreover, although Ukraine remains heavily reliant on its scarce supply of American interceptors to defend against ballistic missile attacks, it is far less dependent on foreign systems and intelligence than it was at the start of the war. The shift to a drone-centered battle space has fundamentally altered combat tactics, the expertise required of soldiers, and the way arms are purchased. It has also rendered some kinds of legacy systems, such as armored vehicles and short-range artillery, increasingly obsolete. Yet it is not the drones themselves that have made the shift so dramatic. To exploit the full potential of unmanned warfare, Ukraine has adopted an integrated digital architecture linking unmanned platforms with situational inputs and intelligence. It has also pursued an unprecedented level of digital coordination, as well as decentralized production and procurement of weapons and of digital technologies themselves. Fedorov was one of the key architects behind the deployment of this drone infrastructure. Unlike many other officials or military leaders, he not only possessed an acute understanding of the battlefield, the weapons deployed in it, and the data streaming from it, but he also had the ability to build, coordinate, and continually upgrade a comprehensive digital system to manage it. Although he served as defense minister for only six months, Fedorov had driven this shift as the head of the Ministry of Digital Transformation, a government agency he created in 2019 and ran until 2026. Drawing on a team of specialists, the agency had set out to replace traditional bureaucratic procedures across government with more efficient digital platforms; a secondary goal was reducing corruption. After Russia’s full-scale invasion, Fedorov’s team became a driving force within the government for Ukraine’s drone program. Since the acquisition of drones initially fell outside formal procurement, the agency was able to largely run the process through its own “Drone Line” initiative. At the same time, it began building a new digital infrastructure to manage drone warfare. Some of these capabilities, such as Delta—a cloud-based system for managing the entire battlefield—had been designed earlier by volunteer-led civic initiatives. But the Ministry of Digital Transformation gave them crucial government support. It also introduced rewards for army units that successfully deployed drones and, later, for those operating unmanned maritime systems and ground robots, as well. Some military analysts worry that these kinds of incentives risk “gamifying” the war or that they oversimplify operational realities. Yet by providing continuous feedback, the programs provide valuable real-time battlefield intelligence, as well as sophisticated data sets for assessing the performance of weapons and units. Fedorov’s team, relying for a time on Zelensky’s backing, pushed for new policies and funding mechanisms to accelerate the military’s digital transformation. It also set out to streamline the military bureaucracy and bring greater transparency to wartime procurement, which has been highly vulnerable to corruption. Over 900 Ukrainian companies now produce thousands of drone models and components. To manage this huge and fragmented sector, the ministry introduced new systems to coordinate logistics, certification, and deployment. Overall, these changes have been significant. Step by step, drones have allowed Ukraine’s armed forces to acquire or sustain capabilities that have traditionally come from missiles and airpower. In 2025, Ukraine had reached parity in the air domain with Russia along the frontline; by 2026, Ukrainian drones and missiles were also able to reach Russian command-and-control centers, cut off logistics, and prevent some Russian assaults. Although Moscow can still outcompete on resources, using oil revenues and vast state spending to finance its aggression, Ukraine’s new digital architecture has enabled it to do more with less, multiplying the effect of particular weapons by connecting sensors, operators, and strike platforms into a unified system. NEW WEAPONS, OLD WAYS Despite their undeniable value, these innovations have often come from outside Ukraine’s military establishment, and sometimes in opposition to it. Overshadowed by the large number of civilian recruits after 2022 is the fact that the Ukrainian army began the war staffed by professional soldiers, with inherited doctrines and lines of command. Although the military established the Unmanned Systems Forces as a separate branch in 2024, its traditional mechanized, infantry, and armored brigades still bore the brunt of the fighting while integrating drones at their own pace. And as with any large national armed forces, the existing hierarchy has resisted wholesale change. Many commanders have embraced drones as weapons—just as they would tanks or guns—yet without fully understanding the structural changes needed to make them effective. Similarly, Ukraine’s established defense industry, which has long counted on existing relationships and contracts, has also resisted the overhaul. Until recently, drone contracting has remained a comparatively small sector. Even though it involves hundreds of millions of dollars, expensive traditional capabilities such as artillery and other conventional weapons systems continue to consume most of Ukraine’s defense budget. Over the past year, however, the balance has shifted: the military’s procurement priorities and the financial interests surrounding them have begun to adjust to drone-centered warfare. And that has created new forms of pushback. Almost from the beginning of his tenure as defense minister, Fedorov and his team were targeted by smear campaigns on anonymous Telegram channels. These have linked him to various military scandals and alleged corruption in the drone industry. Fedorov blames the attacks on entrenched interests—defense contractors and powerful insiders—who were threatened by the shift in war priorities. As one example, he has cited his successful efforts to reduce the price of a procurement deal for short-range artillery that was becoming obsolete, given the expanding kill zones. He also said that Zelensky had received persistent complaints that the digital reformers were breaking a functioning system and disrupting the delivery of essential equipment to frontline troops. At the same time, as large amounts of funding, especially from Ukraine’s international partners, have been directed at drone technology, established defense contractors and well-connected political actors have sought to gain a piece of the pie. They are now moving aggressively to compete with drone startups on drone contracts. Taken together, these tensions brought pressure on Zelensky to move more slowly on the military transformation—which Fedorov had been pushing to accelerate. But the president had failed to understand just how much the public had become invested in Ukraine’s new way of war, and the remarkable results it had begun to achieve. PRESSURE FROM BELOW By the spring of 2026, if defense contractors had misgivings about Fedorov, the Ukrainian public had become increasingly dissatisfied with Syrsky, Ukraine’s commander in chief. Syrsky had notched several strategic victories, including the battle for Kyiv and the liberation of the Kharkiv region during the first year of the all-out war. He had also embraced drone warfare, expanding drone procurement and battlefield integration, although that was part of the army’s broader evolution. Yet many soldiers saw him as a commander who emphasized discipline and was prepared to sacrifice lives when he considered it necessary to achieve a military objective. Within the military, Syrsky had long taken pride in staying close to the frontlines, sometimes to the point of micromanaging the battlefield. But there was also a growing sense among officers and soldiers that he was beginning to value personal loyalty within the command structure above military effectiveness. He had a tendency to sideline talented younger officers and to use his control over promotions and resources to consolidate his own influence. According to some soldiers and officers, these habits risked undermining battlefield readiness, including on the most critical sectors of the front. Then, in June, Ukrainian journalists published a bombshell investigation uncovering horrific allegations of abuse in an assault regiment—a unit that had been given privileged support by Syrsky. The revelations included evidence of violence and unlawful killings within the unit. Although a formal military investigation followed, public criticism remained intense and serving military personnel spoke out. Many laid the blame on Syrsky personally for allowing this to happen. It was after this scandal that Zelensky made the ill-timed decision to fire Fedorov. In the eyes of many Ukrainians, the president was siding with those who opposed reforms. Almost immediately, thousands of people took to the streets of Kyiv and other cities. To contain the public outcry, Zelensky then moved quickly to fire Syrsky and install Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi as his replacement, a choice that was broadly welcomed. Drapatyi, 43, had entered the military in 2014 as a battalion commander and risen through the ranks, while taking part in many defining battles. He is known for embracing new approaches, including the digital battlefield promoted by Fedorov, supporting promising officers, challenging army leaders when necessary, and championing operations that minimize casualties—a priority that Ukrainians value. Meanwhile, Zelensky named Khmara to replace Fedorov. Since 2011, Khmara—in his late 30s or early 40s—had served in Alpha, the Security Service of Ukraine’s special forces unit, and was considered to have an unblemished record. (He had to leave active military service and formally become a civilian before assuming the post, which by law must be held by a civilian.) Yet Zelensky’s moves failed to resolve the underlying tension between the Defense Ministry and the military’s general staff. By law, the defense minister is supposed to nominate the commander in chief to the president. But this time, Zelensky once again effectively selected the commander himself, creating a situation in which the general staff continues to see that it answers to the president, not to the defense minister. LOST MOMENTUM? A larger question is how this political upheaval will affect the war. Fedorov was fired just as the reforms he had been advocating for were helping Ukraine turn the tide against Russia. By spring 2026, Ukrainian long-range drone strikes were beginning to erode one of Russia’s greatest strategic advantages: its oil sector. Kyiv also continued to disrupt Russian logistics in the south, particularly in Crimea, while also attacking oil refineries across the European part of Russia, including Moscow and St. Petersburg. But many wonder whether Fedorov’s dismissal will slow that progress. In Russia, pro-war commentators openly celebrated Zelensky’s decision, viewing it as a rejection of one of the main architects of Ukraine’s military modernization. Hours after his dismissal, representatives of several foreign governments and international technology firms, including the Italian minister of defense and Palantir’s CEO, Alex Karp, offered him positions, which he declined. Zelensky has also offered him several alternative roles in Kyiv, but Fedorov has refused them all because they came with limited decision-making power. Still, he seems almost certain to gain an important place within the government or defense sector sooner or later. Despite Zelensky’s appointment of innovation-minded leaders to replace Fedorov and Syrsky, the future of Ukraine’s digital war ecosystem remains uncertain. Unlike Khmara, who takes office without an established cadre, Fedorov brought to the defense ministry the team he had already built at the Ministry of Digital Transformation. Although only a few of the digitization specialists Fedorov brought to the Defense Ministry have left so far, many more may be pushed out. By calling for elections, Fedorov signaled a move into opposition, raising questions about whether his relationship with Zelensky would deteriorate—and what this would mean for close associates still holding official posts. By design, Ukraine’s digital battlefield infrastructure has the capacity to rapidly evolve in response to changing combat demands. The system can function without Fedorov or his team, but it remains unclear whether it can maintain the pace of evolution needed to stay ahead of Russia. The immediate risk is lost momentum. DEMOCRACY IN THE BALANCE The democratic culture that took hold in Ukraine in 2014 and drove the protests this summer continues to be one of the country’s greatest military strengths. Many of Ukraine’s most important military adaptations have come from below—from individual soldiers and commanders but also from civilian entrepreneurs. Hundreds of private initiatives have advanced technologies, software, manufacturing, and logistics in ways that have dramatically improved the way Ukraine fights. Too many military units, entrepreneurs, engineers, and civic activists are now invested in this ecosystem for a single political decision to dismantle it. But the disruption could affect Ukraine’s ability to iterate new advances on the battlefield—at a moment when the overall dynamic of the war hangs in the balance. For Zelensky, the political damage of his decisions this summer cannot be undone. Ukrainians have largely remained united behind the president in the face of external pressure, including after Donald Trump’s return to the White House in 2025. Nonetheless, he has shown more than once that he is out of step with ordinary Ukrainians. Already a year ago, his effort to restrict the role of Ukraine’s anticorruption authorities provoked major protests and significantly diminished confidence in his leadership. Now, his decision to fire Fedorov has only reinforced that perception. Until this summer, Fedorov had avoided attention, presenting himself as a manager, not a politician. Yet Zelensky’s abrupt decision to dismiss him—for reasons the public still does not understand—made Fedorov one of Ukraine’s most popular figures almost overnight. Now, Fedorov’s call for elections has significantly raised the stakes. In his video address, Fedorov—without mentioning names—again spoke about powerful vested interests that have meddled in government and defense and resisted the changes Ukraine needs to maintain its military advantage. He also asserted that, with no end to the war in sight, Ukraine needs a broader debate about political accountability and decision-making. Clarifying his initially vague but surprising address, the former minister pledged to outline the technical and security logistics of wartime voting—specifically for soldiers, refugees, and frontline residents—to enable a realistic debate on holding elections. Under martial law, elections are barred. Until now, only external powers—Russia or the United States—had questioned Ukraine’s political legitimacy without elections. Most Ukrainians deemed wartime voting dangerous and impractical, fearing that staging elections would simply divert attention, funds, and effort from the front. But Zelensky is in his seventh year as president, under a constitution that permits two consecutive five-year terms. Having made consequential, unpopular decisions, he has increasingly given the sense that he has stopped reading the country’s mood. Fedorov’s announcement may not precipitate an immediate change, but it has started a debate that could play out in the coming months and years. Until now, when it came to the question of holding elections, it had seemed that Ukraine would know when the moment arrived: at some point, in an active, outspoken society, even during war, Ukrainians themselves would demand democratic accountability. This does not mean that Fedorov will automatically gain popularity if he decides to run. His call for wartime voting has alienated some public figures and politicians who backed him as defense minister. They see his intervention now as less a push for accountability than an open political challenge to Zelensky—one that risks draining attention from the reforms that Fedorov had previously championed. With the war likely to continue for the foreseeable future, the urgent question facing the country now is to what degree the people should be given a direct say in the war’s course: how it fights, by what means, according to what strategy, and with what broader vision for its defense. The rise of drone warfare has made military strategy more inclusive, giving a wider range of people—from civil society representatives and tech innovators to members of frontline military units—the expertise and leverage to shape it. That means, on a popular level, more engagement in the war than ever. But for the country’s leaders, it has also created a powerful new set of voices to be reckoned with and be held accountable to—ones that, in the future, may well demand an even greater say. item.title: The End of American Sanctuary
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.44
Among its many advantages, the United States benefits from a rare form of geographic luck: it is bracketed on the east and west by two vast moats, the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, and on the north and south by only two neighbors, both of whom are relatively friendly. Adding to this good fortune is that, since the end of World War II, the United States has possessed a powerful nuclear arsenal and unparalleled military, economic, and technological might. Despite the 9/11 terrorist attacks, this mix of geography, deterrence, and power has led many Americans to feel almost untouchable at home. According to a 2024 Chicago Council on Global Affairs poll, just 19 percent of those surveyed expressed concern about foreign threats. It is time for Americans to revise their assumptions. In fact, the U.S. homeland has never been as vulnerable to attack as it is today. China, Russia, and North Korea are building up their conventional and nuclear capabilities to strike the United States across a variety of domains—and U.S. defenses have not kept pace. A major evolution in technology and tactics, meanwhile, has increased the threat of subversion and gray-zone attacks: drones from state and nonstate actors can strike almost any target in the United States, and adversaries such as China can conduct AI-enabled offensive cyber-operations that can destroy or damage critical infrastructure. The United States is not prepared. The country’s air and missile defenses are porous. Arcane domestic laws and policies prevent the necessary coordination and authority to defend against drone attacks. And energy, water, financial, health-care, and other infrastructure remain vulnerable to advanced cyberattacks. Faced with these new threats, federal, state, and local entities in the United States are caught flat-footed. The 9/11 attacks happened in part because of policymakers’ inability to grasp that the world was changing and to share information across government agencies that could have protected the country. Without an overhaul of the nation’s homeland security apparatus, Washington is in danger of making this mistake again. MISSILES OVER THE MOAT Security measures enacted after September 11 were designed to protect the U.S. homeland from terrorism. The U.S.A. Patriot Act and subsequent legislation enabled U.S. agencies to collect more intelligence at home and abroad. The Department of Homeland Security, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the National Counterterrorism Center, and the Joint Terrorism Task Forces were created or enhanced to better share intelligence about terrorism and other threats. The FBI significantly expanded the number of Joint Terrorism Task Forces across the country, coordinated with state and local law enforcement, and conducted intelligence-led operations to identify and arrest terrorists. These measures were helpful at the time, when terrorism was the biggest threat to the U.S. homeland. And they were successful in preventing the vast majority of terrorist plots in the homeland. But today, some of the greatest threats to the United States come from state actors. China, Russia, and North Korea all possess intercontinental missiles capable of hitting the U.S. homeland—and all have conducted tests and exercises to show that they are capable of using them. The wars in Iran and Ukraine suggest that possessing a nuclear arsenal, even one as large as the U.S. arsenal, no longer protects against conventional attacks on the homeland as it once did. Iran and its network of proxy forces have lobbed tens of thousands of rockets, missiles, and drones at major population centers in Israel. Ukraine has successfully struck Russian cities, energy infrastructure, industrial base targets, logistics nodes, and military bases without incurring a nuclear response from the Kremlin. Advanced Israeli and Russian air and missile defense systems have struggled to stop these drones and missile attacks. In the event of a conventional attack on U.S. soil, American air and missile defense systems might, too. The United States lacks sufficient numbers of air defense systems and interceptors to protect against ballistic missiles. The war with Iran has reduced the military’s global supply of THAAD interceptors by as much as 80 percent and Patriot interceptors by as much as 50 percent. In addition, homeland defense against cruise missiles remains porous. Cruise missiles are difficult to defend against. They fly close to the earth in order to stay below conventional radar, and they use mountains, valleys, and hills to hide from ground-based sensors—what is called “terrain masking.” The United States does not have enough missile defense systems in enough areas to protect against cruise missiles. China especially has expanded and updated its ability to strike the United States. In addition to missiles, the threat from China now extends into space. China can strike targets in the U.S. homeland using a Fractional Orbital Bombardment System, which places a warhead flying at hypersonic speed into low-earth orbit, allowing it to approach the U.S. homeland from an unpredictable direction and bypass traditional early warning radar and missile defense networks. The People’s Liberation Army is also researching other space-based capabilities, such as orbital strike weapons, which would theoretically strike the U.S. homeland by dropping projectiles from space. CHEAP SHOTS The U.S. homeland is also facing novel subversion threats. State and nonstate actors have long used physical sabotage against critical infrastructure, disinformation, and offensive cyber-operations to weaken their adversaries below the threshold of conventional warfare. But new technologies and tactics, including AI, present new challenges for the United States. Drones are the most obvious example. Technological advances have already made drones cheaply and readily available for purchase, with longer ranges, higher payloads, and an improved ability to evade electronic warfare. Adversaries may soon be able to fly drones in coordinated swarms using AI, effectively overwhelming any defenses. Allies and adversaries alike are now engaged in an arms race, ramping up drone production and use in an attempt to innovate their way to the cutting edge. Russia is producing as many as seven million weaponized drones per year. According to some estimates, China has the capacity to build one billion drones per year. It wouldn’t take that much, however, to wreak havoc on the U.S. homeland. In 2025, Ukraine smuggled over 100 drones into Russia inside cargo trucks to conduct strikes that damaged or destroyed roughly one-third of Russia’s active bomber fleet and caused approximately $7 billion in damages. Operation Spider’s Web was a spectacular success for Ukrainian forces—and a chilling reminder of the United States’ susceptibility to a similar attack. An adversary could conceal weaponized drones inside modified cargo vans, shipping containers, or trucks with slidable roofs and position the vehicles near high-value targets, such as military airfields or naval bases, without detection. They could program the drones to launch simultaneously using commercial cellular networks, circumventing domestic air defense and signal-jamming measures and effectively bypassing strategic early warning radar systems. According to some estimates, China has the capacity to build one billion drones per year. Such an attack on U.S. soil might seem far-fetched. But unauthorized drone incursions on U.S. military installations, nuclear power plants, and other critical infrastructure—not to mention outdoor concert venues, sports stadiums, transportation infrastructure, and ports—have been increasing over the past several years. In March, for example, Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana, which houses long-range B-52 bombers, went into lockdown after numerous unauthorized drones were spotted hovering over sensitive areas of the base. In June, the FBI arrested five suspects in an alleged plot to target the Ultimate Fighting Championship event on the White House South Lawn with explosive-laden drones. Artificial intelligence makes individual drones and swarms of drones harder to stop because they do not rely on remote radio signals that can be jammed by electronic countermeasures. Drones are not the only problem made worse by AI’s rapid development. Agentic AI systems such as Anthropic’s Mythos will make it far easier for state and nonstate adversaries, such as terrorists, to penetrate cyberdefenses and attack critical infrastructure at a scale never before possible. Once directed, AI agents can discover flaws in corporate and government computer systems and execute self-directed cyberattacks with minimal human oversight. Even before the advent of these AI systems, the shockingly poor state of national and municipal cyberdefenses made American critical infrastructure an inviting target. Beginning in 2021, China’s Volt Typhoon attacks infiltrated U.S. power grids, water treatment plants, telecommunication systems, and transportation hubs, embedding malware that could sabotage them in the event of a U.S.-Chinese crisis. An AI-enabled Volt Typhoon operation would allow attackers to shift from a slow, human-enabled campaign that takes months or years to a nearly instantaneous, self-adapting campaign against numerous targets simultaneously that could be vastly more damaging. Finally, beyond drones and AI, there is the growing threat of direct-ascent antisatellite weapons, which are missiles launched from the ground, sea, or air that travel into space to strike and destroy a satellite in orbit, as well as directed-energy weapons and electronic warfare systems that can target U.S. satellites in low-earth orbit and geosynchronous orbit. China and Russia are actively developing and testing a broad range of antisatellite and other counterspace weapons. If implemented, such space-based attacks could degrade GPS and navigation, ground commercial flights, and disrupt logistics networks that rely on satellite tracking for freight. In other words, they could at least temporarily grind daily life in the United States to a halt. IMAGINING THE UNIMAGINABLE To better prepare for an attack on the homeland, Washington needs first to fortify the active defenses that protect the country’s critical infrastructure. It needs to build and deploy more upper-range systems like Patriot and THAAD for ballistic missiles, medium-range systems such as the Indirect Fire Protection Capability system for cruise missiles, and short-range systems such as the Coyote and Merops systems to counter drones. Directed-energy weapons—such as high-energy lasers and high-power microwave systems—and radio-frequency jamming and electronic warfare systems are also useful to defend against drone attacks. The United States needs more systems to defend critical infrastructure, as well as training for personnel. It should also ramp up passive defenses, such as digging underground facilities for vital infrastructure and placing high-density and layered concrete barriers around ground systems, power-generation units, ammunition storage facilities, and barracks. Since it would be exorbitantly expensive to protect everything in the homeland, Washington should initially focus on reinforcing critical bases and infrastructure that China or other adversaries could target in a conflict. Key locations include military command-and-control facilities, bomber bases, nuclear weapons sites, air and missile defense systems, and major naval bases. Golden Dome, the Trump administration’s proposed homeland air and missile defense system, can play an important role in this effort. The plan aims to create a unified command-and-control network of sensors, weapons, and other systems to detect and shoot down incoming drones and missiles. But Golden Dome is underfunded and has been slow to get off the ground. Moving forward, the U.S. priority should be accelerating plans to stitch together existing capabilities—not developing new ones—such as the U.S. military’s missile warning satellites; global network of radars and sensors; 44 ground-based interceptors in California and Alaska; and other federal, state, local, and commercial systems. The U.S. military also needs to ramp up live-fire exercises to test Golden Dome’s software and ability to detect, track, and hit incoming threats. Drones present a thornier problem. Commanders at military bases and personnel protecting critical infrastructure often do not have the legal authority to destroy or degrade drones that illegally fly into their airspace. Some recent laws, including the Safer Skies Act of 2025, grant state and local agencies (though not private-sector entities) greater license to detect and track hostile drones. But more comprehensive legislation is needed that allows operators who have received training to deploy and use counterdrone systems under federal or state and local law enforcement supervision. To mitigate the risk that newly empowered operators of counterdrone systems accidentally jam or shoot down civilian aircraft, more state and local personnel should be trained at the National Counter-UAS Training Center in Huntsville, Alabama. The United states can no longer rely on its geography and its nuclear arsenal to protect it. Intelligence sharing among federal, state, and local intelligence agencies improved after 9/11 to disrupt terrorist networks and foil planned attacks. But the evolving nuclear and conventional capabilities of China, Russia, and North Korea, as well as emerging tactics and technology such as drones and AI, make the intelligence practices of the “war on terror” largely obsolete. What’s more, self-inflicted wounds have damaged the few agencies well suited for today’s threats. The Trump administration, for example, has gutted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which oversees cyberdefenses and elections security. The United States needs to establish a robust National Counterintelligence Center, much like the National Counterterrorism Center it established after 9/11, that brings together analysts from multiple agencies to fuse intelligence, analyze threats, and coordinate strategic planning against Chinese, Iranian, Russian, and other threats to the homeland. At the state and local level, the Joint Terrorism Task Forces and Fusion Centers need to shift their focus and resources to tracking state-based threats to the homeland. Finally, the threats currently facing the U.S. homeland require a fundamental shift in mindset. U.S. policymakers, the country’s security establishment, and its citizens must recognize that the United States is in a new era; it can no longer rely on its geography and its nuclear arsenal to protect it. Finland, Israel, and Ukraine have long traditions of developing strategic plans and communicating to their publics about homeland threats. The United States should follow suit by educating the American public about the evolving threats to the homeland and developing a national resilience plan—much as Finland has done—to harden critical infrastructure, closely collaborate with the private sector, adapt laws, and communicate with the public. Americans’ overwhelming sense of safety was briefly and tragically shaken by the attacks on September 11, 2001, and the 9/11 Commission went on to argue that the United States faced a “generational challenge” from terrorist groups. A quarter century later, there is a new generation of Americans and a new generational challenge. If the 9/11 attacks were in large measure a failure of imagination and implementation, as the commission wrote, Washington risks repeating that same mistake today. item.title: The End of Thailand’s Long Stalemate?
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.42
For more than 25 years, Thailand’s conservative establishment and opposition forces have been locked in a struggle for the soul of the country. Royalists want palace institutions insulated from public criticism, a military licensed to intervene in times of political crisis, deferential political parties and politicians, and free rein to clamp down on political actors who fail to toe the line. The opposition calls for a constitutional monarchy, a military that stays in the barracks, a competitive party system responsive to the people’s wishes, and predictable checks and balances that do not unduly punish elected politicians. More often than not, the royalists have had the upper hand. They have mobilized protest movements, staged military coups, and banned opposition parties to prevent troublesome politicians from instituting changes that could limit their power and privileges. Yet every attempt to strike a decisive blow against the opposition has failed. Conservatives have not translated legal or extralegal victories into lasting governments. Opposition movements, meanwhile, have consistently reinvented themselves. Thaksin Shinawatra, the larger-than-life former policeman and telecom billionaire, built up enormous power as prime minister in the early 2000s, incurring the disdain of royalists. And even after a military coup removed Thaksin from the premiership in 2006, his parties remained electoral juggernauts. A yet more alarming challenge emerged on the horizon after a 2014 coup ousted Thaksin’s sister, Yingluck Shinawatra, from government: youth-based mass protests calling for reform of the monarchy in 2020 and progressive political parties who appealed to these younger voters. A stalemate had prevailed over Thai politics, with neither side able to overpower the other fully. That changed in February 2026, when Bhumjaithai, a low-profile party previously known primarily for campaigning to legalize cannabis, swept into power in national elections. With the implicit backing of the monarchy and the conservative establishment, Bhumjaithai has seized control of the Thai state, giving rise to a new mode of politics capable of both suppressing progressive forces in favour of cozy collaboration among elites and winning a general election without overt manipulation. Far from an electoral anomaly, the rise of Bhumjaithai is the culmination of a long effort by conservatives to retake the levers of power. In fact, the formerly also-ran party’s February triumph was part of a methodical, behind-the-scenes campaign to commandeer the state’s nominally neutral apparatuses, including its Senate and Constitutional Court. The alliance between the monarchical network and Bhumjaithai is more a marriage of convenience than a shared ideological project, and it may not last indefinitely. But shallow as it may be, it has already succeeded in decisively strengthening the conservative position, disempowering the major rival parties that threaten elite control, and potentially remaking the Thai state for years to come. RAINBOW COALITIONS The origins of Thailand’s current political order date back to 1997, when a group of elite liberal royalists, claiming a mandate from civil society, introduced a landmark new charter. Often referred to as “the people’s constitution,” it was a reaction to a disastrous military coup in 1991 and its bloody aftermath, including the deadly suppression of unarmed protesters in May 1992. The reforms aimed to coup-proof the political system by introducing checks and balances to prevent elected politicians from abusing their power and facilitate a smooth royal succession. It established an electoral commission, a constitutional court, an anticorruption agency, and a human rights commission, as well as a fully elected, purportedly nonpartisan Senate. The project backfired. It failed to stabilize Thai politics—probably an unrealistic goal to begin with—and the new parliamentary system allowed for the election of Thaksin as prime minister in 2001. A charismatic figure with populist authoritarian tendencies, he successfully mobilized lower-income voters in the heavily populated north and northeast regions of Thailand, melding them into an unbeatable electoral bloc. He used his considerable personal wealth, his party’s parliamentary dominance, and his bureaucratic connections to create a startlingly successful political machine. Thaksin bought off the Senate and the independent agencies, defanging them as neutral bodies, and installed loyalists in crucial posts intended to check the prime minister’s power. The country’s traditional elites were deeply threatened by Thaksin’s ascendance. The so-called Yellow Shirt movement, which appropriated a royal color, sought to make Thailand ungovernable. Through mass street protests and the occupation of public spaces and buildings, it paralyzed opposition rule three times: in 2006, 2008, and in 2013–14. But for all its success in ousting opposition-led governments, the Yellow Shirt movement never solved a basic problem: conservatives could bring down an elected government, but they couldn’t win an election to replace it. Conservatives were unable to tolerate ambitious, independent-minded administrations. The 2006 and 2014 political crises initially followed a similar pattern. Street protests destabilized and delegitimized Shinawatra-led governments, and military coups then removed them. Each time, the establishment brought in the Royal Thai Army to reorganize politics, rewrite the constitution, and reconfigure the party system in its favor before holding fresh elections. But military force failed to bring about durable conservative rule. Coups were short-term fixes that gradually eroded the legitimacy of the establishment. The Thai public was willing to tolerate only short interludes of military rule, and coup makers had no choice but to promise the imminent restoration of democracy. Generals, however, were bad at politics. The public quickly tired of them, and voters soon welcomed back the same kinds of politicians that soldiers had kicked out. In the 2007 elections, the first called by the ruling junta after the 2006 coup, for instance, Thaksin’s party was voted back into power. The experience was imprinted on the minds of conservatives when they launched the 2014 coup; the new government postponed elections until 2019. The inability of conservatives to break the opposition once and for all persuaded the establishment to try to cut deals with Thaksin’s Pheu Thai Party instead. A strategy of conciliation permitted the opposition to front a government as long as party leaders concentrated on managing the economy and did not challenge the special status of the monarchy. Pheu Thai, conservatives believed, could always be co-opted or browbeaten into a politics of benefit sharing in which wealth and power were divided between a Pheu Thai figurehead and conservative power brokers. This was the deal behind Yingluck Shinawatra’s administration of 2011 to 2014, an arrangement that both conservatives and Thaksin supporters found unsatisfying and were reluctant to acknowledge. But government by veto was inherently unstable. Eventually, the conservatives were unable to tolerate ambitious, independent-minded Pheu Thai administrations and brought them crashing down, as they did in the 2014 military coup. Where they did not want to use force, they turned to lawfare to limit the opposition’s power. Starting in 2019, a series of more progressive “orange” opposition parties proved wildly popular, especially among younger voters. After the orange Move Forward Party won the largest number of seats in Thailand’s National Assembly in the 2023 elections, the military-appointed Senate blocked its leader, Pita Limjaroenrat, from assuming the premiership. The following year, Move Forward was summarily dissolved—the fifth major opposition party to meet this fate—and the Constitutional Court banned Pita from political office for ten years. By 2025, the establishment was running out of options to disempower the opposition. Challenged by both pro-Thaksin forces and progressive orange parties, its old methods—military coups, dodgy deals, party bans, the judicial removal of prime ministers—were wearing thin. Conservatives desperately needed an alliance with a reliably deferential party that could win elections. HOLLOW PARTY Enter Bhumjaithai, a previously medium-sized party based in the northeastern province of Buriram. The product of a breakaway by a faction of members of parliament and former ministers from Thaksin’s party in 2008, Bhumjaithai had for the first 17 years of its existence no popular politicians among its ranks, no clear economic policies, and no national following. Yet under the guidance of the shadowy Newin Chidchob, Bhumjaithai has gradually become a force in Thai politics and a crucial ally of the monarchy and its sympathizers. Known euphemistically by the party faithful as “the school principal,” Newin served as a junior minister under Thaksin and in other governments but stepped back from frontline politics two decades ago, ostensibly to concentrate on building up his Buriram United soccer team. He neither grants interviews nor appears in public but exercises tight control over Bhumjaithai’s strategy and personnel. Current Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, a U.S.-trained engineer and former deputy minister whose family owns the massive Sino-Thai Engineering and Construction company, has served as the party’s leader and public face since 2012. What Newin and Anutin lack in ideological vision, they have made up for in strategic cunning, accumulating power wherever possible and making themselves useful to the monarchical network. Correctly diagnosing the establishment’s desperate need for a reliable political party with which to collaborate, they set out to distinguish their party from other conservative contenders, which were typically packed with reliable but often underperforming former bureaucrats. To do so, Newin and Anutin transformed Bhumjaithai into a major vehicle for influential provincial business interests. Control of the key ministries was a crucial first step in the project to capture state power. As a precondition to joining coalition governments as a junior partner, Bhumjaithai demanded ministerial positions that would help it secure stronger local networks. In 2019, Anutin became minister of public health and subsequently boosted the pay of over one million health volunteers in villages across the country. Anutin’s support turned many of them into canvassers for Bhumjaithai—an electoral masterstroke, given that Thai elections are often won and lost in these provincial areas, where vote-canvasser networks are all-important. Then, in 2023, Bhumjaithai secured control of the powerful Ministry of Interior, which oversees local governance in Thailand, including more than 70,000 village headmen. In the right hands, the Interior Ministry can be a formidable patronage machine, exerting authority over everything from local budgets to Senate elections. The party then combined the health and headmen networks to penetrate every community in Thailand. Today, Anutin still holds the post of interior minister, in addition to his position as prime minister. Other behind-closed-doors moves solidified Bhumjaithai’s power. For most Thai citizens, the selection of 200 new senators in 2024 through an arcane and untested self-nomination system barely registered, creating ample opportunity for manipulation. Candidates linked to Bhumjaithai gamed the system and secured around two-thirds of the supposedly neutral upper chamber—a majority that has allowed conservative forces to quietly block independent-minded candidates for the Constitutional Court, the Election Commission, and the Anticorruption Commission and to exercise veto power over any future changes to the constitution. Missteps by the opposition also smoothed the path for the party’s ultimate takeover of the state. When the Bhumjaithai-controlled Constitutional Court removed Thaksin’s daughter, Paetongtarn Shinawatra, as prime minister in August 2025, the orange party—now known as the People’s Party—voted for Anutin, rather than another Pheu Thai member, to replace her. People’s Party leaders naively believed a Bhumjaithai government would be in office for only a brief period and that after winning an early election, progressive forces could push to amend the constitution and reduce the entrenched power of the elite. This was a disastrous miscalculation. In the February election, Bhumjaithai shocked most observers by decisively topping the polls, winning 192 seats to the People’s Party’s 120 seats. With Bhumjaithai in control of both the internal levers of power and parliament, the prospects for progressive constitutional reform evaporated. SAME AS IT EVER WAS? By neutralizing the Pheu Thai and the People’s Party, Bhumjaithai has made itself the most successful conservative party in modern Thai history. Far from transforming the country’s politics, however, this dominance has ground it to a halt. The incarnation of transactional conservatism, Bhumjaithai now controls every major mechanism of the state. But whereas in the past the various royalist and opposition factions jockeying for influence each stood for something tangible, the party is a cipher, favored by many conservatives, yet largely devoid of ideological or policy content or an organic base of support. Today, a country known for mobilizing millions of people around big ideas, both during hotly contested elections and through massive extraparliamentary movements, is led by a party with no apparent ideas at all. The political reform project that began in the 1990s has run its course. So, too, have Thaksin’s project to empower the disadvantaged, the military’s nationalist project to restore order and defend the monarchy, and the progressive project to transform Thailand into a more open and equal place. At the same time, Bhumjaithai’s vacuous opportunism reflects a new form of realpolitik that appears much more durable than previous iterations. Royalists have grudgingly rallied around the party because they have nowhere else to go. Thaksin, recently chastened by an eight-month prison term, has gone quiet. Progressives criticize and deconstruct what they decry as the “blue regime” (after the color of Bhumjaithai’s logo) but struggle to articulate a realistic strategy to challenge it. Despite the contradictions that underpin Anutin’s government, it has shown no sign of imminent collapse. This hollow dominance has yielded a strange impasse. For the last six months, Anutin’s administration has mostly treaded water, postponing major initiatives. That impasse may not hold as younger generations become a force in Thai politics. Indeed, conservatives’ grip on power remains deeply contested and contingent. A united opposition that puts aside the long-standing differences between pro-Thaksin and progressive forces could in theory topple Bhumjaithai at the ballot box. A return to Move Forward’s winning slogan in 2023—a Thailand that is “not the same as before,” code for the dismantling of gerontocracy and unearned privilege across the country’s creaking structures and institutions—could serve as the basis for an alternative administration. But even if an anti-Bhumjaithai coalition were to take back power, it would struggle to unwind the party’s control of Thailand’s political institutions. However long Bhumjaithai’s present tenure in Bangkok lasts, that takeover of the levers of state power will be its enduring legacy.
